title: DOJ’s 20,000 “Likely” Noncitizen List in California Includes U.S.-Born Residents, NPR Reports
body:
Election officials in Los Angeles County have raised serious doubts about a federal list that the Justice Department says identifies roughly 20,000 voters in California who are “likely” non‑citizens. After a preliminary review of the data, the county’s election department concluded that the list is “unreliable” and that many of the names appear to belong to U.S.–born residents, casting fresh doubt on the Justice Department’s demand that California separate those ballots from the rest of the vote count.

The Department of Justice, citing a 2020 voter‑registration database compiled by the federal government, has asked California to take the unprecedented step of segregating and reviewing ballots associated with the 20,000 individuals it believes may be ineligible to vote. The request, which would require election officials to set aside those ballots for additional scrutiny, has sparked a fierce legal and political battle. California’s Attorney General’s office has already filed a lawsuit challenging the request, arguing that the federal list violates state law and the Constitution by imposing an undue burden on the voting process.

Los Angeles County’s initial analysis, released in a brief statement, found that a significant portion of the names on the list are linked to people who were born in the United States, have long‑standing voting histories, or are otherwise documented as eligible citizens. “Our early findings suggest the data set contains numerous false positives,” the county’s chief elections officer said. “If the state were to act on this list, it could disenfranchise thousands of lawful voters.” The county’s audit compared the federal list with state voter registration records, driver‑license data, and other public databases, uncovering discrepancies that point to methodological flaws in how the Justice Department compiled the list.

Legal experts say the controversy highlights a broader clash between federal immigration enforcement and state election autonomy. The Justice Department’s approach stems from a 2020 federal directive that urged states to identify and remove non‑citizen voters, a policy that many states, including California, have resisted as unnecessary and politically motivated. “The federal government has no legal authority to dictate how states conduct their elections, especially when the underlying data is demonstrably unreliable,” said a professor of election law at a California university. “Any attempt to purge or segregate ballots based on such a list would likely run afoul of the Voting Rights Act and the Fourteenth Amendment.”

Political ramifications are already evident. Republican leaders at the federal level have lauded the Justice Department’s effort as a necessary safeguard against voter fraud, while Democratic officials in California have framed the move as an attack on voting rights. Governor Gavin Newsom, in a recent press conference, warned that “using flawed data to suppress legitimate votes is a direct threat to our democracy.” Meanwhile, advocacy groups for immigrant rights have mobilized to monitor the situation, urging voters to report any irregularities and offering legal assistance to those who might be mistakenly targeted.

The dispute is expected to head to court in the coming weeks, with both sides preparing extensive evidence. The Justice Department says it will refine its methodology and provide additional documentation to support the list’s accuracy, while California officials plan to conduct a more thorough, independent audit before any action is taken. If the courts ultimately side with the federal government, the state could be compelled to implement a ballot‑segregation process that would delay vote tabulation and potentially erode public confidence in the electoral system.

As the 2026 midterm elections approach, the outcome of this legal battle could set a precedent for how, or whether, the federal government can influence state voter‑registration practices. For now, election officials in Los Angeles County remain cautious, emphasizing that protecting the integrity of the vote must not come at the expense of disenfranchising legitimate voters. The next steps will likely hinge on judicial rulings that balance national security concerns with the constitutional right to vote, a balance that will shape the future of American elections.
